mcqs.question: Why does each VendingState method return the next state instead of the machine checking if (state == X) before acting?
options: It makes insertMoney() run faster
Each state class only needs to implement the transitions legal from it, so illegal ones become clean no-ops or are simply absent instead of being guarded by scattered conditionals
It removes the need for an Inventory class
It guarantees the machine can never run out of change
mcqs.explanation: The State pattern's payoff is that 'what's legal from here' lives inside each state class instead of being checked at every call site. It has no effect on raw method speed, doesn't touch Inventory, and doesn't prevent running out of change (that's ChangeMaker's job).

mcqs.question: Why does a greedy 'always pick the largest coin that fits' algorithm risk failing to make exact change?
options: Greedy algorithms are always slower than dynamic programming
It only works for amounts under one dollar
With some denomination sets, or when a denomination is running low in the dispenser, greedy can get stuck needing an amount no remaining coin can cover, even though a different combination would work
Greedy algorithms cannot be implemented in Java
mcqs.explanation: Greedy fails whenever the available denominations (or what's left in a real dispenser) don't line up with its assumptions, leaving a remainder no coin can cover even though another combination succeeds. Speed isn't the issue here, it's not amount-limited, and the language is irrelevant.

mcqs.question: What's the main risk of implementing the vending machine's lifecycle as an enum field plus switch statements instead of the State pattern?
options: A missed or outdated case in one of the switch statements compiles fine and can silently produce wrong behavior, and the legality check is duplicated across every method
Switch statements execute more slowly than interface dispatch in virtually all cases
Enums cannot represent more than four values
It would require removing the Inventory class
mcqs.explanation: The real risk with switch-on-enum is maintainability and silent bugs: a forgotten case compiles and can misbehave, and 'is this legal now' logic is duplicated everywhere the switch appears. Performance and enum size limits aren't the actual concern, and Inventory is unrelated.

mcqs.question: A background restocking job reads Inventory while a purchase is mid-flight decrementing it. What actually fixes the race?
options: Pause all restocking jobs permanently, since inventory should never be read live
Have the restocking job simply retry until the numbers look stable
Move the decrement logic into the state machine's transition instead of Inventory
Make Inventory.decrement(slotCode) an atomic operation, so a concurrent read never observes an in-between state and a competing write can't be lost
mcqs.explanation: The fix is the same shape as any shared-mutable-state race: make the mutation atomic so readers never see a torn update and writers can't silently clobber each other. Banning restocking isn't practical, retrying doesn't fix a race condition, and moving the code elsewhere doesn't make it atomic.

mcqs.question: Why should HasMoneyState call machine.addFunds(amount) instead of directly setting machine.balance += amount?
options: Direct field access is not supported in Java
It keeps the invariant of how balance may legally change in one place (Machine), instead of scattered across every state class that might touch it
It makes the machine dispense the product faster
It's required so ChangeMaker can access the balance
mcqs.explanation: Routing mutation through Machine's own API keeps 'how balance can change' as one invariant in one place, so bugs like double-crediting are easier to find and prevent. Java allows direct field access; this doesn't affect dispense speed; and ChangeMaker doesn't need this path to read a balance.
